\chapter{Character, Not Mood}
\label{ch:hi-character}
\hlchaptermodality{91}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what a person is like rather than how they feel today, using seven disposition adjectives and predicting from the ending alone which of them change for a woman.}

Answer the question what is he or she like, noticing that kaisaa itself bends, so the gender is announced in the question before any adjective arrives.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[burā]{\hi{बुरा} — bad, and the phrase you will hear it in first}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-buraa}



\begin{quote}
You have had \emph{acchā} for a long time and have never had its opposite. Say it, then notice that you cannot yet say the other thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बुरा}}
\textbf{\hi{बुरा}} (\emph{burā}) — \textquotedblleft{}bad.\textquotedblright{}

It ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, so by now you know without being told: \emph{burā}, \emph{burī}, \emph{bure}. The shape rule you learned about size words works on character words too, because it was never about meaning.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{बुरा}} is the word inside one of the most-heard sentences in everyday Hindi:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{बुरा} \hi{मत} \hi{मानो}} — \emph{burā mat māno} — \textquotedblleft{}don't take it badly.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Literally: \emph{do not consider it bad}. It is what a speaker adds after saying something blunt, and it is closer to English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}no offence\textquotedblright{}} than to any apology. You will hear it long before you need to produce it, so recognising it is worth more right now than being able to build it.

A second everyday one: \textbf{\hi{बुरा} \hi{लगना}} — \emph{burā lagnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to feel hurt,\textquotedblright{} literally \emph{to strike one as bad}. Hindi describes being offended as something the remark does, not something you do.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a pair that behaves identically}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\emph{acchā} & \emph{acchā} & \emph{acchī} \\
\hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरी} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both inherited, both ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, both bending. The pair is the easiest one in the chapter, and the rest of the chapter is where it stops being easy: four of the six words ahead do \textbf{not} bend.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{बुरा}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{burā}, bad
  \item the feminine form (\emph{burī})
  \item \emph{acchā aur burā} — the pair
  \item what \emph{burā mat māno} means (roughly, \textquotedblleft{}no offence\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{बुरा} \hi{मत} \hi{मानो}} literally say? (Do not consider it bad.) Does \textbf{\hi{बुरा}} bend? (Yes — it ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.) And \textbf{\hi{मोटा}}, from the last chapter? (Also yes — same ending, same behaviour.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hośiyār]{\hi{होशियार} — holding your wits, which is a compliment and a warning at once}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-hoshiyaar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{आसान}}. It ends in a consonant and never bends. The word in this lesson ends in a consonant too — so predict what it will do before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{होशियार}}
\textbf{\hi{होशियार}} (\emph{hośiyār}) — \textquotedblleft{}clever, sharp, alert.\textquotedblright{}

It ends in \textbf{\hi{र}}, a consonant, so it does not bend. \emph{Ek hośiyār laṛkā}, \emph{ek hośiyār laṛkī} — the adjective is the same shape for both.

\begin{cousinweb}
Persian, and built from two pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{होश}} (\emph{hoś}) — consciousness, one's senses, one's wits
  \item \textbf{-\hi{यार}} (\emph{-yār}) — holding, keeping
\end{itemize}

So a \emph{hośiyār} person is one who \textbf{keeps hold of their senses}. Not one who knows a great deal — one who is \emph{awake}.

That is why the word does double duty. Called out sharply, \textbf{\hi{होशियार}!} means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}look out!\textquotedblright{}} — the Indian Railways used it as the standard shouted warning. The same word praises a bright child and stops a man walking into a moving cart, because both are about being alert.

\textbf{\hi{होश}} on its own is worth keeping. \emph{Hoś meṅ ānā} is \textquotedblleft{}to come to one's senses,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{hoś uṛnā} is literally \textquotedblleft{}for one's wits to fly away\textquotedblright{} — to be stunned.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the first one that does not bend}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरी} \\
\hi{होशियार} & \hi{होशियार} & \hi{होशियार} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The difference is not that one is about character and the other about worth. It is the last letter, and nothing else. \textbf{\hi{बुरा}} is inherited and ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}; \textbf{\hi{होशियार}} is Persian and ends in a consonant.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{होशियार}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hośiyār}, clever
  \item the form you would use about a woman (the same one)
  \item what \textbf{\hi{होशियार}!} shouted on a platform means (\emph{look out})
  \item what the two pieces of the word mean (\emph{wits} and \emph{holding})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{होश}} mean on its own? (One's senses or wits.) Why does \textbf{\hi{होशियार}} not bend? (It ends in a consonant, not in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mehnatī]{\hi{मेहनती} — an ending that makes a person out of a thing}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-mehnati}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{होशियार}}. It ends in a consonant and stays put. This word ends in \textbf{-\hi{ई}}, which is a third shape, and it also stays put — for a different reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मेहनती}}
\textbf{\hi{मेहनती}} (\emph{mehnatī}) — \textquotedblleft{}hard-working, industrious.\textquotedblright{}

It is built out of a noun you can see inside it: \textbf{\hi{मेहनत}} (\emph{mehnat}), \textquotedblleft{}hard work, toil,\textquotedblright{} plus the ending \textbf{-\hi{ई}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मेहनत}} is Arabic \emph{miḥna}, which did not start out meaning honest labour. It meant a \textbf{trial, an ordeal, a testing} — the thing that puts a person through it. Work became the name for the ordeal, which is a judgement about work that several languages independently agreed on.

The \textbf{-\hi{ई}} on the end is one of the most useful endings in Hindi. Attach it to a noun and you get \emph{the person characterised by that thing}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{the person} \\
\midrule
\hi{मेहनत} — toil & \hi{मेहनती} — one who toils \\
\hi{शरम} — shame & \hi{शर्मीला} — one who feels it \\
\hi{ज़रूरत} — need & \hi{ज़रूरी} — necessary \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is the same job English does with \textbf{-y} in \emph{wealthy}, \emph{greedy}, \emph{speedy} — and, in fact, the very same job Persian does with \textbf{-ī} in \emph{Hindī}, \textquotedblleft{}belonging to Hind.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third shape, and why it also stays put}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{changes for a woman?} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\hi{आ}} & \hi{बुरा} & yes, to \textbf{-\hi{ई}} \\
consonant & \hi{होशियार} & no \\
\textbf{-\hi{ई}} & \hi{मेहनती} & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The reason the third row does not move is worth seeing rather than memorising: the feminine ending an \textbf{-\hi{आ}} adjective changes \emph{to} is \textbf{-\hi{ई}}. A word that already ends in \textbf{-\hi{ई}} has nowhere to go. It is not an exception — it is the rule arriving at a word that is already there.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मेहनती}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mehnatī}, hard-working
  \item the noun hiding inside it (\emph{mehnat})
  \item the feminine form (the same one — it already ends in \textbf{-\hi{ई}})
  \item \emph{hośiyār aur mehnatī} — clever and hard-working, neither one moving
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Arabic \emph{miḥna} mean before it meant work? (A trial or ordeal.) Why does an \textbf{-\hi{ई}} adjective not change for a woman? (\textbf{-\hi{ई}} is already the feminine ending; there is nowhere further to go.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śarmīlā]{\hi{शर्मीला} — the ending that turns a feeling into a character}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-sharmeela}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{मेहनती}}. You saw an ending build a person out of a noun. The same thing happens here with a different ending, and this one bends.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{शर्मीला}}
\textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} (\emph{śarmīlā}) — \textquotedblleft{}shy, bashful.\textquotedblright{}

Built from \textbf{\hi{शरम}} / \textbf{\hi{शर्म}} (\emph{śaram}), \textquotedblleft{}shame, modesty,\textquotedblright{} plus the ending \textbf{-\hi{ईला}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The ending \textbf{-\hi{ईला}} is not the same as the \textbf{-\hi{ई}} of \emph{mehnatī}, and the difference is exactly the difference this chapter is about.

\textbf{-\hi{ई}} says \emph{has this thing}. \textbf{-\hi{ईला}} says \emph{is made of this thing} — it builds a settled quality, a disposition rather than an episode:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{with \textbf{-\hi{ईला}}} \\
\midrule
\hi{शरम} — shame & \hi{शर्मीला} — shy by nature \\
\hi{रंग} — colour & \hi{रंगीला} — colourful, flamboyant \\
\hi{नशा} — intoxication & \hi{नशीला} — intoxicating \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is why \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} is the right word for an exam question about character. Someone can \emph{feel} shame at a moment; a \emph{śarmīlā} person is one for whom it is a standing trait. This is settled character, not mood — the distinction the whole chapter turns on.

\textbf{\hi{शर्म}} itself is Persian, and it is the same word as English \textbf{shame}: both descend from the same ancient root for covering oneself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: back to the bending shape}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरा} & \hi{बुरी} \\
\hi{मेहनती} & \hi{मेहनती} & \hi{मेहनती} \\
\hi{शर्मीला} & \hi{शर्मीला} & \hi{शर्मीली} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-\hi{ईला}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, so the rule applies as usual and the word bends. The long ending does not protect it: look at the \textbf{last letter}, always.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{शर्मीला}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{śarmīlā}, shy
  \item the feminine form (\emph{śarmīlī})
  \item the noun inside it (\emph{śaram})
  \item the difference between feeling ashamed once and being \emph{śarmīlā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the ending \textbf{-\hi{ईला}} add that \textbf{-\hi{ई}} does not? (A settled quality rather than merely having the thing.) Does \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} bend? (Yes — it ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[milansār]{\hi{मिलनसार} — the opposite of shy, built out of a word you have had for ages}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-milansaar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}}. Now think of the opposite kind of person — the one who is easy with strangers. Hindi builds that word out of something you learned in order to say goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मिलनसार}}
\textbf{\hi{मिलनसार}} (\emph{milansār}) — \textquotedblleft{}sociable, friendly, easy to get on with.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
Two pieces, and you already have the first:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मिलन}} (\emph{milan}) — a meeting, from \textbf{\hi{मिलना}}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} — the verb inside \emph{phir milenge}, the farewell you learned early
  \item \textbf{-\hi{सार}} (\emph{-sār}) — a Persian ending meaning \emph{inclined toward, full of}
\end{itemize}

So a \emph{milansār} person is \textbf{inclined toward meeting}. Hindi names the trait after the act rather than after the feeling, which is a plainer way to describe a person than English manages: \emph{sociable} goes back to Latin \emph{socius}, a companion, and is a noun about a relationship; \emph{milansār} is a verb about what someone actually does.

The \textbf{-\hi{सार}} ending is rare enough to be worth flagging as a small set rather than a rule to apply. You will meet \textbf{\hi{शर्मसार}} (\emph{śarmsār}), \textquotedblleft{}ashamed\textquotedblright{} — built on the same \emph{śaram} as the last lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a consonant ending, so it stands still}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\hi{शर्मीला} & \hi{शर्मीला} & \hi{शर्मीली} \\
\hi{होशियार} & \hi{होशियार} & \hi{होशियार} \\
\hi{मिलनसार} & \hi{मिलनसार} & \hi{मिलनसार} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The pair \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} / \textbf{\hi{मिलनसार}} is the sharpest demonstration in the chapter: two opposite traits, and one bends while the other does not. Meaning has nothing to do with it. Only the last letter does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मिलनसार}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{milansār}, sociable
  \item the verb hiding inside it (\emph{milnā}, to meet)
  \item the form for a woman (the same one)
  \item \emph{śarmīlā aur milansār} — and hear that only the first one could move
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is inside \textbf{\hi{मिलनसार}}? (\emph{Milnā}, to meet.) Why does it not bend while \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} does? (It ends in a consonant; \textbf{\hi{शर्मीला}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gambhīr]{\hi{गंभीर} — deep, which is how three separate languages say serious}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-gambhir}



\begin{quote}
You learned that \textbf{\hi{मोटा}} describes a \emph{deep} voice. Hold on to that idea of depth — this lesson takes it somewhere else entirely.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{गंभीर}}
\textbf{\hi{गंभीर}} (\emph{gambhīr}) — \textquotedblleft{}serious, grave, solemn.\textquotedblright{}

It ends in \textbf{\hi{र}}, a consonant, so it does not bend.

\begin{cousinweb}
Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{गम्भीर}}, and its first meaning was \textbf{deep} — of water, of a well, of a voice.

What is striking is how many unrelated languages reached for \emph{depth} or \emph{weight} when they needed a word for gravity of manner:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{word} & \textbf{first meaning} \\
\midrule
Hindi & \hi{गंभीर} & deep \\
Latin & gravis & heavy \\
English & profound & deep \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A serious person, in all three, is one you cannot see the bottom of. Hindi still uses the literal sense freely: a \emph{gambhīr} river is a deep one, and a \emph{gambhīr} illness is a grave one.

One useful distinction, and it is the same one English draws. A \emph{gambhīr} person is solemn and weighty. A \emph{gambhīr} situation is dangerous. The word does not decide which; the noun does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: all six, sorted by ending}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{the words} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\hi{आ}} & \hi{बुरा}, \hi{शर्मीला} & \hi{बुरी}, \hi{शर्मीली} \\
consonant & \hi{होशियार}, \hi{मिलनसार}, \hi{गंभीर} & unchanged \\
\textbf{-\hi{ई}} & \hi{मेहनती} & unchanged \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two bend and four do not, and you can sort them without knowing what a single one means.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{गंभीर}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{gambhīr}, serious
  \item the form for a woman (the same one)
  \item \emph{gambhīr aur mehnatī} — two words, neither one moving
  \item what a \textbf{\hi{गंभीर}} river is (a deep one)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\hi{गंभीर}} first mean? (Deep.) Which Latin word for heavy took the same path to \textquotedblleft{}serious\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Gravis}.) Does it bend? (No — it ends in a consonant.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāt śabd svabhāv ke]{\hi{सात} \hi{शब्द} \hi{स्वभाव} \hi{के} — seven words, three endings, and one pair of opposites}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-repaso-svabhaav}



\begin{quote}
Name as many of the seven as you can before reading the table. Aim for five.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending decides, and the meaning never does}]
All seven, sorted by what their last letters allow:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
\emph{acchā} & good & \emph{acchī} \\
\hi{बुरा} & bad & \hi{बुरी} \\
\hi{शर्मीला} & shy & \hi{शर्मीली} \\
\hi{होशियार} & clever & \hi{होशियार} \\
\hi{मिलनसार} & sociable & \hi{मिलनसार} \\
\hi{गंभीर} & serious & \hi{गंभीर} \\
\hi{मेहनती} & hard-working & \hi{मेहनती} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the third column against the first. Where the two differ, the word moves for a woman; where they are identical, it does not. Three move and four stay.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where each word came from}]
The split is not random, and seeing why makes the endings predictable:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{source} & \textbf{the words} & \textbf{ends in} \\
\midrule
inherited from Sanskrit & \emph{acchā}, \hi{बुरा}, \hi{गंभीर} & mostly \textbf{-\hi{आ}} \\
Persian & \hi{होशियार}, \hi{मिलनसार}, \hi{शर्मीला} & mostly a consonant \\
Arabic through Persian & \hi{मेहनती} & \textbf{-\hi{ई}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Inherited words are the ones that kept the \textbf{-\hi{आ}} ending, because they are the ones that went through the whole sound history of the language. Borrowed words arrived later, in whatever shape the lending language had them, and mostly that shape ended in a consonant.

\textbf{\hi{गंभीर}} is the exception that proves it is a tendency rather than a law: it is inherited from Sanskrit and still ends in a consonant. So the origin explains the pattern — the \textbf{ending} is what you act on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three that move, in their feminine forms
  \item the four that stay put
  \item the one pair of outright opposites (\emph{acchā} and \emph{burā})
  \item the two that describe how a person is with strangers (\emph{śarmīlā} and \emph{milansār})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the seven is inherited and still refuses to bend? (\textbf{\hi{गंभीर}}.) Why does \textbf{\hi{मेहनती}} not bend? (It already ends in \textbf{-\hi{ई}}, which is where a bending adjective would go.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vah kaisī hai?]{\hi{वह} \hi{कैसी} \hi{है}? — the question the seven were assembled to answer}

\label{lesson:HI-C83-sintesis-svabhaav}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{होशियार}} and \textbf{\hi{मेहनती}}. Two words no reference letter could do without, and the track had neither until now.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question word bends too}]
\textbf{\hi{कैसा}} is itself an \textbf{-\hi{आ}} word, so the question agrees before the answer does:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{about} & \textbf{question} & \textbf{a possible answer} \\
\midrule
a man & \hi{वह} \hi{कैसा} \hi{है}? & \hi{वह} \hi{गंभीर} \hi{है।} \\
a woman & \hi{वह} \hi{कैसी} \hi{है}? & \hi{वह} \hi{शर्मीली} \hi{है।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice what that means in practice. The gender is announced \textbf{in the question}, before any adjective arrives. A listener who catches only \emph{kaisī} already knows a woman is being asked about — and knows that any bending adjective in the answer must end in \textbf{-\hi{ई}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read aloud. Every word has been taught:

\begin{quote}
— \hi{आपकी} \hi{बहन} \hi{कैसी} \hi{है}? — \hi{वह} \hi{होशियार} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{मेहनती} \hi{भी} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{शर्मीली} \hi{है।} — \hi{आपका} \hi{भाई} \hi{कैसा} \hi{है}? — \hi{वह} \hi{मिलनसार} \hi{है।} \hi{वह} \hi{गंभीर} \hi{भी} \hi{है।}
\end{quote}

Five adjectives in that exchange, and only \textbf{\hi{शर्मीली}} had to change its ending. The other four were decided by their own last letters rather than by who was being described — which is the entire point of the chapter, put into one conversation.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{कैसी} \hi{है}?\textquotedblright{} and answer it with two of the seven
  \item the same answer about a man, changing only what can change
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वह} \hi{मिलनसार} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{} and then the feminine version, and hear that nothing moved
  \item \emph{acchā} and \emph{burā}, the one outright pair of opposites among the seven
  \item one sentence about somebody you know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \textbf{\hi{वह} \hi{कैसी} \hi{है}?}, what has already told you a woman is being asked about? (The question word itself — \textbf{\hi{कैसी}}, not \textbf{\hi{कैसा}}.) Which adjectives in the answer would have to follow suit? (Only the ones ending in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
